Neurology · published research

Diabetic neuropathy

Recent trials reported lower neuropathic pain or improved protective sensation after PBM, while an earlier double-blind trial found monochromatic infrared treatment no better than sham for sensory neuropathy. The clinical results therefore remain mixed.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Recent trials reported lower neuropathic pain or improved protective sensation after PBM, while an earlier double-blind trial found monochromatic infrared treatment no better than sham for sensory neuropathy. The clinical results therefore remain mixed.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact diabetic-neuropathy category contains 42 unique titles: 27 human research reports, six animal publications and nine review, meta-analysis or protocol titles. Human reports include 16 randomized trials and 11 other controlled, non-randomized, single-arm or retrospective studies. The review and protocol labels overlap in the source inventory, so type subtotals are not additive. Reviews synthesize existing trials rather than providing new patient cohorts.

Human and clinical evidence

Recent randomized studies report positive short-term outcomes. Oggiam et al. randomized 168 participants with painful diabetic polyneuropathy, with 144 completing follow-up. Their 890-nm monochromatic infrared-light group reported lower pain after six weeks and at a later assessment, as well as better sleep quality (Oggiam et al. 2024). Anju et al. randomized 200 people with type 2 diabetes and peripheral neuropathy and reported reduced symptoms and pain, improved protective sensation and better quality of life after a short treatment course (Anju et al. 2025). In contrast, a 69-person double-blind sham-controlled trial found that monochromatic infrared photoenergy did not improve sensory neuropathy more than sham (Lavery et al. 2008). Other small studies include both positive and null results. The meta-analysis in the database judged evidence for pain relief limited and low certainty (Robinson et al. 2017).

Animal evidence

Six animal publications examine nerve function, pain behavior or tissue markers in diabetic models. They support biological questions about nerve response but do not resolve patient benefit.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo publication was identified in this exact category. Biomarker assays within patient studies are not separate laboratory experiments.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols range from visible red laser treatment around 633 nm to near-infrared or infrared systems around 810–890 nm. Some use small laser probes on the feet, while monochromatic infrared energy uses pads over the limbs. Schedules range from several days to 12 weeks, and reported power and fluence are inconsistent. These device, site and schedule differences make the trial results difficult to combine as one treatment.

Interpretation

The evidence supports possible short-term pain or sensory improvement for some protocols, but blinded trials disagree and lasting nerve recovery has not been established. Recent positive findings need independent replication with reliable sham controls, clear dosage reporting and follow-up long enough to determine whether symptom gains persist.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term pain relief and sensory change because some randomized trials are positive while other sham-controlled trials are null. Very low for durable nerve recovery, ulcer prevention or disease modification.
Publications and records42 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The largest recent trials report short-term symptom or sensory improvement, but older blinded MIRE studies found no advantage over sham and protocols differ substantially. Reviews also identify low certainty for several outcomes. Future trials should use credible sham devices, validated pain and nerve measures, report dosimetry fully and follow participants after treatment ends.
